The whole molecule likely is aspirin? Aspirin is C9H8O4, has benzene ring with acetoxy group (O-CO-CH3) and a carboxylic acid. SMILES for aspirin: "CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O". Let's verify fragments: benzene ring C1=CC=CC=C1 matches aromatic core. CC(=O)O is acetate (CH3-CO-O). In aspirin, the acetyl group attached via O to aromatic: O-COCH3. That's CC(=O)O attached to O. The fragment C(=O)O is carboxylic acid attached directly to aromatic. So overall SMILES: "CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O". That matches formula C9H8O4. Unique carbon environments: aromatic 6, carbonyl carbon of acetate, carbonyl carbon of acid, methyl carbon = 9 unique. Hydrogen environments: aromatic protons (maybe 4 distinct due to substitution pattern), methyl protons, acidic OH, maybe aromatic? Actually aspirin has 4 aromatic H (positions 3,4,5,6) all equivalent? In para? Actually aspirin is ortho? The ring has two substituents ortho? Aspirin is acetylated salicylic acid: salicylic acid has OH ortho to COOH; aspirin replaces OH with OCOCH3, so substituents are ortho: one is OCOCH3, other is COOH. That gives 4 aromatic H, each distinct? Might be 4 unique. So matches.

Thus answer SMILES: CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O
